components.description: Benchmark objective for pouring two non-Newtonian liquids of different densities: pour the light blue liquid out of the glass while retaining as much white heavy liquid as possible.
components.grounding_note: No declared class specifically represents a task objective or selective-liquid retention goal; an objective is not a strategy.

candidates.reviewer_note: Provisional benchmark-scoped objective, not evidence of successful execution or a general pouring strategy.

source_support.exact_quote:
Fined Grained Pouring A glass filled with two types of non-Newtonian liquid with different densities, colored as blue and white respectively. The task is to pour the light blue liquid out of the glass
while retaining as much white heavy liquid as possible.

candidates.statement: In FluidLab's fine-grained pouring task, defined for a glass containing two non-Newtonian liquids of different densities, the objective is to pour out the light blue liquid while retaining as much white heavy liquid as possible.

components.description: Pouring loss specification: sum particle-to-goal distances for upper-layer fluid particles using the ground location as the goal, and add a loss attracting lower-layer fluid particles to their initial positions.
components.grounding_note: The supplied classes do not explicitly represent a benchmark loss specification; this metric definition is not itself an observed outcome.

candidates.reviewer_note: Provisional metric description. No equivalence between the layer labels here and the color labels in the task passage is asserted.

source_support.exact_quote:
Transporting, Pouring, Gathering (Easy) and Gathering (Hard): These tasks use a single spatial
location as the goal and the loss is computed as: L = Σi kpi − pgoal k, which is summed over all
particles of the object(s) to be manipulated. For Pouring, we apply this loss between the particles
of the upper layer fluid and the ground location, with an additional loss attracting the particles of the
lower layer fluid to their initial positions.

candidates.statement: For FluidLab's Pouring benchmark, the loss applies the stated summed particle-to-goal distance loss to upper-layer fluid particles relative to the ground location, with an additional loss attracting lower-layer fluid particles to their initial positions.

components.description: Reported CMA-ES performance pattern in the evaluated FluidLab setup: reasonable performance on many simple-spatial-goal tasks, but difficulty with fine-grained control tasks including pouring.

Reported DP-H performance pattern in the evaluated FluidLab setup: gradient-based trajectory optimization without the Section 5.1 techniques does similarly well on relatively simple settings but fails to produce good trajectories for more complex, non-convex tasks including fine-grained Pouring.

candidates.reviewer_note: Provisional source-reported performance patterns, not universal method limitations or independently corroborated causal claims.

source_support.exact_quote:
Sampling-based trajectory optimization CMA-ES does reasonably well in many tasks with simple
spatial configuration as goals. However, it struggles in fine-grained shape matching tasks (e.g. Ice
Cream) and fine-grained control tasks (e.g. pouring). This is because CMA-ES searches for action
sequences via trajectory sampling, and thus cannot handle delicate interactions well.
Differentiable physics-based trajectory optimization In most of the tasks, the gradients provided
by our differentiable simulation are able to guide trajectory optimization towards a good optimization spot, resulting in near-oracle performance. It also demonstrates better sample-efficiency than
8

 Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2023

other methods in most tasks. We additionally compare with a hard version of differentiable physics
(DP-H), which uses the gradient to optimize trajectory, but without using the optimization techniques proposed in Section 5.1. DP-H does similarly well on tasks with relatively simple settings,
but fails to produce good trajectories in scenarios with interactions between fluids and other materials bodies, as well as in tasks with more complex and non-convex optimization landscapes, such
as Pouring with fine-grained control objective. The experimental results demonstrate that the gradient information provided by our differentiable simulator, coupled with the optimization schemes we
proposed, provides informative optimization information when dealing with complex fluid systems.

candidates.statement: Under FluidLab's reported evaluated conditions, CMA-ES does reasonably well on many tasks with simple spatial goals but struggles with fine-grained control tasks such as pouring. DP-H, which optimizes trajectories using gradients without the Section 5.1 optimization techniques, does similarly well on relatively simple settings but fails to produce good trajectories on more complex, non-convex tasks such as Pouring with a fine-grained control objective.
